bp: Public language-model systems need a fast way to stop a harmful request before the model starts answering. The ordinary object here is a user prompt: a piece of text that may be a legitimate question, or may be a jailbreak, meaning wording crafted to push the model around its safety rules. Many deployed defenses look at the prompt from the outside. They try to recognize harmful intent, spot suspicious surface features, or ask a separate classifier to judge the input or output. PADD starts from a different observation: the base model already has internal signals about what parts of a prompt it is using. If a safety reminder is placed in front of the same prompt, a benign request and an adversarial request should disturb those internal focus patterns differently. The paper serves web-scale safety because it tries to make attack detection early, lightweight, and usable without retraining or changing the protected model.
wh: The hard part is that jailbreaks are designed to look unlike the dangerous request they carry. An attacker can change wording, add indirection, wrap the request in a role-play, or make small perturbations so a surface scanner sees something less suspicious. A post-generation defense has another problem: it spends computation producing an answer before deciding whether the answer should be blocked. A separate classifier can help, but it adds cost and may learn the same shallow clues that attackers can avoid. Modifying or fine-tuning the base model is also expensive and may not fit systems that need to protect several existing open-source models. The deeper tension is that the defense must notice intent without depending only on the prompt's outer wording. It must also be quick enough to run before generation. PADD's challenge is therefore to turn the model's own reaction to the prompt into a safety signal that separates benign from adversarial cases.
naive: A smart beginner would put a filter in front of the model. The filter would block prompts with dangerous words, known jailbreak phrases, or patterns that resemble earlier attacks. If that missed cases, the beginner might add an external classifier trained on benign and adversarial examples, or check the generated answer afterward. Those moves are reasonable because they match the visible evidence. They fail when the attack hides the visible evidence. Subtle prompt changes can leave the harmful instruction understandable to the model while making it unfamiliar to the filter. Output checking also pays the cost of generation and may be too late for low-latency systems. The beginner is checking the surface of the prompt, while the useful evidence may be in how the model internally reacts to safety pressure.
ap: PADD's central move is to create a controlled comparison for each prompt. It runs the prompt in its original form and also with a lightweight safety prefix placed before it. A prefix is just a short added instruction or reminder; here its purpose is to make the model consider safety before reading the user request. PADD then compares attention distributions, where attention means the model's internal allocation of focus across parts of the text while it is processing the prompt. It also measures attention plasticity, meaning how easily that focus pattern changes when the safety prefix is added. Instead of asking whether this prompt looks like a known attack, PADD asks whether this prompt behaves strangely when safety context is introduced. The abstract says this turns cross-prompt comparison into self-comparison: the prompt is mainly judged against its own prefixed version, not against a distant library of examples.
mech: The mechanism begins with one user prompt. First, PADD lets the base language model process the prompt normally and records the model's attention distribution, the pattern of how much internal focus different prompt parts receive. Second, PADD creates a second version of the same input by prepending a lightweight safety prefix. The abstract does not give the exact prefix text, so the safe claim is only that it is a short safety-oriented addition meant to nudge the model toward safety-relevant processing. Third, the same base model processes this prefixed prompt, again producing internal attention signals. Fourth, PADD compares the two runs. One signal is attention divergence: how far the focus pattern moved after the prefix was added. Another is attention plasticity: how responsive or bendable the focus pattern is under that prefix. Fifth, PADD combines these signals into a detector score. If the original and prefixed versions remain close in the way benign prompts tend to remain close, the prompt is allowed through. If the safety prefix causes a distinctive shift that separates the prompt from benign behavior, the prompt is flagged before generation. The output is a pre-generation safety decision. The important engineering point is that PADD does not fine-tune model weights, add a separate external judge, or wait for harmful content to be produced.
math: The main mathematical ideas are controlled comparison, distribution distance, classification, and cost-aware detection. A distribution is a set of shares that add up to a whole: in this paper, it describes how the model's internal focus is spread across prompt parts. Divergence means measuring how different two such spreads are. If the focus before and after the safety prefix is nearly the same, the distance is small; if focus moves sharply to different prompt regions, the distance is large. Plasticity adds a second view: not merely where focus moved, but how sensitive the model's focus is to the prefix. The classification problem is then to draw a boundary between benign and adversarial prompts using these composite signals. This is mathematical because the detector must compress many internal focus values into a score and choose a threshold where attacks are caught while normal users are not rejected. The tradeoff is missed attacks versus false rejection, with latency as a third constraint. PADD's self-comparison is also important: comparing a prompt to its own prefixed version controls for much of the prompt's topic and wording, so the measured change is more directly tied to how safety context alters processing.
dots: Within the repo's current data, this paper sits in the LLM security thread and the broader privacy, federated, and security family, where many papers ask what hidden signal crosses a boundary and how to detect it before damage occurs. PADD's boundary is the moment before generation: the system must decide whether a prompt may pass into answer production. It connects closely to RepMism, which studies a mismatch between input guardrails and the core model; PADD answers from the defender side by looking inside the model rather than trusting a separate surface reader. It also neighbors SpatialJB, where harmful meaning is hidden across layout, because both papers show that attacks can evade ordinary textual checks while remaining meaningful to the model. Prompt Forensics is another sibling: it studies safety evidence after interactions happen, while PADD tries to use internal evidence early enough to block the interaction.
ww: PADD should work when adversarial prompts disturb the model's safety-sensitive processing differently from normal prompts. A benign user request may change somewhat when a safety prefix is added, but the added reminder should not overturn the model's basic reading of the request. A jailbreak is different. Its wording is trying to steer the model away from ordinary safety behavior, hide intent, or make the unsafe continuation feel permissible. When the same request is prefixed with safety context, the model may redistribute focus in a more dramatic or more bendable way because the prefix conflicts with the adversarial pressure already present in the prompt. That gives PADD a signal that a surface classifier might miss. The self-comparison matters because it avoids relying only on a catalog of known attacks. The method asks, for this exact prompt, whether adding safety context exposes an unstable internal reaction. The reported low attack success rates and low false rejection rates support the idea that this internal change is more separable than raw wording alone, at least across the tested open-source models and public benchmarks.
po: The payoff is a practical pre-generation guard that can be attached to existing large language models. The abstract reports experiments across four mainstream open-source models and multiple public benchmarks. PADD reduces attack success rates to 0.4 to 3.0 percent while keeping false rejection rates between 0 and 5.2 percent. That means the detector is not only catching many jailbreaks; it is also, in the reported settings, rarely blocking benign prompts. Because it uses internal model signals and avoids base-model modification or fine-tuning, the promised capability is low-latency protection that can be deployed without rebuilding the model.
limits: Several assumptions must hold. The base model must expose attention signals, and those signals must differ consistently enough between benign and adversarial prompts after the safety prefix is added. The safety prefix must be lightweight but still strong enough to reveal the contrast. The abstract reports results on four mainstream open-source models and public benchmarks, but that does not prove transfer to closed models, future model architectures, multilingual prompts, layout-based attacks, tool-using agents, or adaptive attackers who design prompts specifically to keep attention divergence small. The abstract also does not specify the exact prefix, scoring formula, threshold choice, or latency numbers. PADD detects before generation; it does not by itself prove that every harmful output path is blocked.
